claims.source: Direction changes at the boundary of two media in the described oblique case.
Some light energy returns to the first medium: reflection.
A transparent second medium can transmit some light across the boundary under suitable conditions, with the described change of direction.
This boundary transmission phenomenon is refraction.
Refraction changes apparent size, shape and position.
Simple observation can demonstrate this.
Small coin/object at empty glass bottom; align coin center, rim and eye by moving glass.
Keep head fixed while filling; rising water makes bottom/coin appear higher, and formerly partial coin becomes wholly visible.
Oblique pencil in water: top view apparently broken near surface, submerged end apparently raised; figure151.
Side view: submerged part displaced sideways and diameter apparently enlarged; figure152.
Boundary direction change explains the observations.
Ray approaching boundary through first medium is incident ray.
Alpha is incidence angle measured from interface normal at point of incidence.
Ray in second medium is refracted ray; beta is its angle to the same normal; figure153.
Visible narrow beam allows incident/reflected/refracted relative positions to be determined.
Little smoke in air or a screen at a small angle to beam reveals path.
Colored fluorescent aquarium water shows refracted beam; figure154.
Refraction angle increases when incidence angle increases in the observed transmitting case.
The two angles are not directly proportional.
Seventeenth-century experimental law: incident ray, refracted ray and interface normal are coplanar; sine-incidence/sine-refraction ratio constant for given media.
Alpha incidence, beta refraction; sin(alpha)/sin(beta)=n, equation6.8.
n is relative index, second medium relative to first, not inverse.
Medium relative to vacuum defines absolute refractive index.
For vacuum-to-medium light, absolute index equals sine-incidence/sine-refraction ratio.
n=n2/n1, second/first absolute index, equation6.9; proof promised in chapter7.
Snell ratio sin(alpha)/sin(beta)=n2/n1, equation6.10.
Smaller absolute index means optically less dense.
Absolute index has physical significance.
Connected to light propagation speed and medium state: temperature, density, elastic forces/stress.
Index also depends on light properties.
Red index smaller than green, green smaller than violet in the described materials.
Index tables often specify light color and medium state; when omitted, their effects are treated as negligible for use of those values.
Common interfaces are air-solid/air-liquid rather than vacuum-medium; solid/liquid absolute and air-relative indices differ little.
Standard-state yellow-light air absolute index approximately1.000292; n=n2/n1 approximately n2.
Table lists some materials' indices relative to air for yellow light.
Transparent semicylindrical glass with frosted back tests refraction law.
Mount on disk with coincident block/disk centers; figure155.
Light follows disk radius and refracts at block flat face; frosted back reveals route.
Move light source to vary incidence angle.
Graduations measure incidence and refraction angles.
Trigonometric tables verify constant sine ratio as incidence varies.
Observed refraction angle is smaller than incidence angle in this air-to-glass/water experiment.
Rearrange6.8: sin(beta)=(1/n)sin(alpha), equation6.11.
Glass/water relative to air n>1 =>1/n<1=>sin(beta)<sin(alpha)=>beta<alpha for nonzero oblique acute angles.
Entry to optically denser medium bends toward interface normal.
Normal incidence alpha0 is undeviated with beta0.
Refracted beam does not carry all incident energy in this experiment.
Some energy reflects into first medium, air.
Change alpha from0degrees normal incidence toward90degrees horizontal/grazing.
Reflection angle changes from0 to90degrees by reflection law.
Observed reflected intensity increases with incidence angle.
Nearly horizontal beam reflects almost entirely from water or glass.

independentModernScienceQuestions: Refraction need not change ray direction at normal incidence.
All ratio equations need nonzero-angle domain; zero/zero is not a number.6.11 itself is valid at normal incidence.
Relative/absolute indices must retain correct medium direction and noninverted n2/n1.
Color and physical-state dependence must remain; optical density must not mean mass density.
Visible red/green/violet ordering is a normal-dispersion applicability statement, not universal across absorbing/anomalous bands.
1.000292 must retain standard-state yellow-light and approximate status.
Strict beta<alpha is limited to nonzero oblique air-to-glass/water acute-angle transmission, not normal incidence or arbitrary medium order.
Observed reflected-intensity trend requires adequate material/polarization/incident-intensity scope; the90degree grazing limit is not total internal reflection.
